title: The Dhammapada in the world
hook: carried across Asia in Pali, Gandhari, Sanskrit and Chinese; Max Müller brought it into English in 1870

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dhammapada, and your line: yours. Did you get to ten? Which one surprised you? Day two hundred thirty.

In the eighteen nineties, in the desert near Khotan, on the old Silk Road in what is now western China, a French expedition came away with pieces of a very old manuscript. It was written on birch bark, in a script few people could read, in a language of the old northwest of India. When scholars finally worked it out, they found verses they knew. Here, far from where the Pali canon was kept, someone had carried the same sayings you've been reading. Today: the Dhammapada in the world.
screen: `BIRCH BARK NEAR KHOTAN.` → `A SCRIPT FEW COULD READ.` → `VERSES THEY KNEW.`

segments.voice: The version we've read is the Pali Dhammapada, kept by the Theravada tradition of Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia. But it has cousins. That birch-bark manuscript is called the Gandhari Dharmapada, after Gandhara, the region of today's northern Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan where its language was spoken. Another version survives in a mixed Indian language and is named after the city of Patna. A larger Sanskrit collection called the Udanavarga, used by other early schools, shares many verses with it and was later translated into Tibetan. And the sayings went into Chinese early, in the third century, where they were read in monasteries. The collections don't match exactly. Chapters are arranged differently, some verses are missing, some are added. What's striking is how much stays the same across languages and centuries: hatred ending by not-hatred, the mind coming first, the bee and the flower. Then the verses traveled west. A Danish scholar, Viggo Fausböll, published the Pali text in Europe with a Latin translation in the eighteen fifties. Max Müller brought it into English in eighteen seventy and revised it in eighteen eighty-one for the series the Sacred Books of the East, the version we've read. Since then many more translations have followed, and the book is still read by Buddhists and by people of other paths. Each of those carried it: monks memorizing on foot, scribes on birch bark, translators at desks. And now you, if you pass one verse along.
screen: `THE PALI, AND ITS COUSINS.` · `GANDHARI, PATNA, SANSKRIT, CHINESE.` · `SO MUCH STAYS THE SAME.` · `FAUSBÖLL, THEN MÜLLER, 1870.` · then, large: `WHO ELSE CARRIED IT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Picture the long line of people who carried these verses to you. A monk walking a mountain road, reciting under his breath. A scribe in Gandhara, writing on bark. A translator in China, searching for the right word. A scholar in Oxford with his lamp. Then you, here. Now choose one verse from your ten, and think of one person who might like to hear it. You're next in the line. The bell holds the time.

Gandhari Dharmapada. A birch-bark manuscript found near Khotan, a cousin of the Pali text: the sayings were carried in Pali, Gandhari, Sanskrit, Chinese and Tibetan, then into English in eighteen seventy.
Your line: who else carried it. Today, share one verse from your ten with one person, simply, and join the line. Day two hundred thirty.

howItsDone: The Pali Dhammapada is chanted and studied throughout Theravada Buddhism; related collections were kept by other early schools, and Tibetan and East Asian Buddhists know the sayings through the Udanavarga and Chinese versions.

original.note: Pali dhammapada; in Gandhari and Sanskrit the same title is dharmapada.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Dhammapada is one fixed book.
what it means: a family of collections carried across Asia, sharing most of their verses.
what a scholar hears: the Khotan birch bark (Dutreuil de Rhins expedition, 1890s) is in Kharosthi script; Chinese versions include the Faju jing of the third century.

notes: Gandhari Dharmapada: birch-bark manuscript in Kharosthi script, acquired near Khotan in 1892 by the Dutreuil de Rhins mission (parts also went to Russia via Petrovsky); confirm date and wording 'a French expedition came away with pieces'.
Patna Dharmapada language is often described as a hybrid Prakrit; 'a mixed Indian language' used.
Chinese: the Faju jing (T 210), translated c. 224 CE (Wei Qinan / Zhi Qian); confirm 'third century'.
Fausböll's edition with Latin translation: 1855; the teach says 'the eighteen fifties'.
Müller's 1870 English appeared with Rogers's 'Buddhaghosha's Parables'; revised 1881 for SBE 10.
'A scholar in Oxford with his lamp' in the practice is an image, not a documented detail.

Editor review 2026-10-01: softened unsupported counts and superlatives ('hundreds of verses', 'dozens of translations', 'thousands of miles', 'for centuries', 'great series'); Kharosthi described as a script few could read rather than almost nobody.
